<!-- mainone-1: body_md -->
Let $\beta=2$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textnormal{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
\item Every $\boldsymbol{\upsilon}\in\boldsymbol{\Upsilon}_b$ determines a determinantal process
$\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}_{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}$ with kernel $\mathfrak K_{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}$ on $(0,\tau(\boldsymbol{\upsilon}))$, obtainable as
a finite-dimensional limit of finite unscaled Dyson Brownian motions.
If $\boldsymbol{\upsilon}^{(N)}\to\boldsymbol{\upsilon}$, their kernels converge locally uniformly in the
spatial variables at each fixed finite collection of positive times below
$\tau(\boldsymbol{\upsilon})$, and the corresponding processes converge in finite-dimensional
distributions.
\item With the root data $\boldsymbol{\xi}$ fixed, write $\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}^{\gamma_1,\gamma_2}$ for the
process with the indicated scalar parameters. Put $A_t=1-\gamma_2t$ and
$\Phi_t(x)=A_tx-\gamma_1t$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:intro-parameter-map}
 \left(\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}^{\gamma_1,\gamma_2}\left(t\right)\right)_{0<t<1/\gamma_2}
 \overset{\mathrm{law}}{=}
 \left(\left(\Phi_t\right)_\#
 \boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}^{0,0}\left(t/A_t\right)\right)_{0<t<1/\gamma_2}.
\end{equation}
\item Under the path hypotheses above, including
\eqref{eq:intro-separation}, the limiting parameter has $\gamma_2=0$.
The processes have continuous versions with their prescribed configurations
at time zero, and convergence holds in
$\mathcal C([0,\infty)\to\mathfrak M)$.
\item For either of the two Markov classes above, $\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}$ has the
Markov property, with transition laws given by restarting the same
construction from the current configuration.
\item Under \eqref{eq:intro-relaxation-data}, as $T\to\infty$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:intro-sine-limit}
 \left(x\mapsto x/\sigma_T\right)_\#
 \boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\left(T+\sigma_T^2t\right)
  \overset{\mathrm{f.d.d.}}{\longrightarrow}\ \boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}_{\mathsf{Sine},\rho_q}\left(t\right)
\end{equation}
in finite-dimensional distributions at fixed real rescaled times. The difference between the rescaled kernel and the limiting extended sine
kernel tends to zero locally uniformly in all four variables.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end mainone-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Proposition~\ref{well_defined process} gives the construction and finite-particle
realisation, and Theorem~\ref{MainTheorem} gives parameter continuity.
Proposition~\ref{gammadependence} proves (ii), and
Theorem~\ref{theorem path cts} proves (iii). The two assertions in (iv)
are Corollaries~\ref{cor:section5-markov} and~\ref{xi in L have M-p}.
Finally, (v) is Theorem~\ref{thm:main}.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- maintwo-1: body_md -->
Let $\beta\geq1$ and suppose the regularity and approximation assumptions
above hold. Construct the finite Dyson systems from $\mathbf{x}^{(N)}$ using
the common Brownian family $(\mathsf{B}_i)_{i\in\mathbb Z}$. Then, almost surely,
each fixed coordinate converges uniformly on compact time intervals to
the unique strong solution $\boldsymbol{\mathsf{X}}=(\mathsf{X}_i)_{i\in \mathbb{Z}}$, among processes with gap process in
$\mathcal P_{\kappa,\rho}^p$, of
\begin{equation}\label{eq:intro-shifted-isde}
 \mathrm{d}\mathsf{X}_i\left(t\right)=\mathrm{d}\mathsf{B}_i\left(t\right)
 +\frac\beta2\left\{\mu_i\left(\boldsymbol{\mathsf{X}}\left(t\right)\right)
 -\gamma\right\}\mathrm{d} t,
 \qquad\mathsf{X}_i\left(0\right)=x_i,\quad i\in\mathbb Z.
\end{equation}
Pathwise uniqueness holds among adapted solutions in this regular class.
Moreover, $\mathsf{S}^{(N)}\to\mathsf{S}_{\cdot,\gamma}$ locally uniformly on
$[0,\infty)\times\mathbb H$ almost surely, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:intro-stieltjes}
 \mathrm{d}\mathsf{S}_{t,\gamma}\left(z\right)=\mathrm{d}\mathsf{U}_t\left(z\right)
 +\left\{\frac\beta4\partial_z\left(\mathsf{S}_{t,\gamma}\left(z\right)^2\right)
 +\frac{2-\beta}{4}\partial_z^2\mathsf{S}_{t,\gamma}\left(z\right)\right\}\mathrm{d} t,
\end{equation}
where $\mathsf{U}$ is a holomorphic local-martingale field with the covariations
specified in Proposition~\ref{prop:stieltjes-spde}.
<!-- end maintwo-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Theorem~\ref{theo sde theorem} gives the coupled particle convergence and
the strong existence and pathwise uniqueness statements.
Proposition~\ref{prop s transform convergence} identifies the limit of
the finite Stieltjes transforms, and Proposition~\ref{prop:stieltjes-spde}
gives its stochastic evolution and covariations.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
We denote by $\mathfrak{M}$ the space of nonnegative, locally finite,
integer-valued Radon measures on $\mathbb{R}$. Thus every
$\boldsymbol{\xi}\in\mathfrak{M}$ can be written as
\begin{equation*}
    \boldsymbol{\xi}=\sum_{i\in I}\delta_{x_i},
\end{equation*}
where $I$ is at most countable, repetitions among the $x_i$ are allowed,
and $\boldsymbol{\xi}(K)<\infty$ for every compact $K\subset\mathbb{R}$. We say that
$\boldsymbol{\xi}^{(N)}$ converges vaguely to $\boldsymbol{\xi}$, and write
$\boldsymbol{\xi}^{(N)}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{vg}}\boldsymbol{\xi}$, if
\begin{equation*}
    \lim_{N\to\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}}f\,\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\xi}^{\left(N\right)}
    =\int_{\mathbb{R}}f\,\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\xi}
    \qquad\text{for every }f\in\mathcal{C}_c\left(\mathbb{R}\right).
\end{equation*}
Equipped with the vague topology, $\mathfrak{M}$ is a Polish space
(see, for example, \cite{article}).
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
For $T>0$, let $\mathcal C([0,T]\to\mathfrak M)$ be the space of continuous
paths, equipped with the metric
\begin{equation*}
    d_{\mathcal C,T}\left(\phi,\psi\right)
    \overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}\sup_{t\in\left[0,T\right]}d_{\mathrm{vg}}\left(\phi\left(t\right),\psi\left(t\right)\right).
\end{equation*}
Then $\mathcal{C}([0,T]\to\mathfrak{M})$ is Polish; see
\cite[Theorem~4.19]{Kechris1995}.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
The topology of locally uniform convergence on
$\mathcal{C}([0,\infty)\to\mathfrak{M})$ is induced by
\begin{equation*}
    d_{\mathcal C}\left(\phi,\psi\right)
    \overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}2^{-n}
      \min\left\{1,\sup_{t\in\left[0,n\right]}d_{\mathrm{vg}}\left(\phi\left(t\right),\psi\left(t\right)\right)\right\}.
\end{equation*}
Convergence for this metric is equivalent to convergence in
$\mathcal{C}([0,T]\to\mathfrak{M})$ for every $T>0$.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
Let $\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}$ be a random configuration with the point-process law under consideration,
and let $\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}_n$ be its factorial measure as in \eqref{Xi_n}.
The $n$-th correlation measure is
\[
    M_n\left(A\right)\overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}\mathbb{E}\left[\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}_n\left(A\right)\right],\qquad A\in\mathcal{B}\left(\Lambda^n\right).
\]
If $M_n$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\lambda^{\otimes n}$,
we denote its density by $\rho_n$:
\[
    M_n\left(A\right)=\int_A\rho_n\left(x_1,\ldots,x_n\right)
    \prod_{j=1}^{n}\lambda\left(\mathrm{d} x_j\right).
\]
The function $\rho_n$ is called the $n$-th correlation function.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop criterion rho determine bxi}
For every relatively compact Borel set $B\subset\Lambda$, put
\[
    m_n\left(B\right)\overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}\frac{1}{n!}\int_{B^n}\rho_n\left(x_1,\ldots,x_n\right)
    \prod_{j=1}^{n}\lambda\left(\mathrm{d} x_j\right).
\]
If, for every such $B$, there exists $C_B<\infty$ such that
\[
    m_n\left(B\right)\leq C_B^n n^n,\qquad n\in\mathbb{N},
\]
then the correlation functions determine the point process uniquely.
In particular, it is sufficient that
\[
    \sup_{\left(x_1,\ldots,x_n\right)\in B^n}\left|\rho_n\left(x_1,\ldots,x_n\right)\right|
    \leq C_B^n n^{2n},\qquad n\in\mathbb{N}.
\]
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{determinantal}
A point process on $\Lambda$ is called determinantal if there exists a
measurable, locally bounded kernel
$\mathfrak K:\Lambda\times\Lambda\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq rho and kernel}
    \rho_n\left(x_1,\ldots,x_n\right)
    =\det\left[\mathfrak K\left(x_i,x_j\right)\right]_{i,j=1}^{n},\qquad n\in\mathbb{N}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{remark bounded K determines process}
If $B\subset\Lambda$ is relatively compact and
\[
    \left\|\mathfrak K\right\|_B\overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}\sup_{x,y\in B}\left|\mathfrak K\left(x,y\right)\right|,
\]
then Hadamard's inequality gives
\[
    \sup_{\left(x_1,\ldots,x_n\right)\in B^n}\left|\rho_n\left(x_1,\ldots,x_n\right)\right|
    \leq\left\|\mathfrak K\right\|_B^n n^{n/2}.
\]
Thus a locally bounded determinantal kernel determines the process
uniquely by Proposition~\ref{prop criterion rho determine bxi}.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
\label{def time-dependent process}
Let $\mathcal I\subset\mathbb{R}$. An $\mathfrak{M}$-valued process
$\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}=(\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}(t))_{t\in\mathcal I}$ is called
determinantal with extended kernel $\mathfrak K$ if, for every finite set
$\mathcal A=\{t_1,\ldots,t_M\}\subset\mathcal I$, the configuration
\[
    \sum_{m=1}^{M}\delta_{t_m}\otimes\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}\left(t_m\right)
\]
on $\mathcal A\times\mathbb{R}$ is determinantal, with reference measure
equal to counting measure on $\mathcal A$ times Lebesgue measure on
$\mathbb{R}$, and with kernel equal to the restriction of $\mathfrak K$.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
\label{def weakly finite dim}
For $\mathfrak M$-valued processes $\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}^{(N)}$ and $\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}$ on $\mathcal I$,
we write $\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}^{(N)}(\cdot)\xrightarrow{\mathrm{f.d.d.}}\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}(\cdot)$ if
their joint laws at every finite collection of times in $\mathcal I$
converge weakly in the corresponding finite product of $\mathfrak M$.
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop mgf convergence}
Let $\mathcal I\subset\mathbb{R}$ and let $\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}^{(N)}$ be
determinantal processes with extended kernels $\mathfrak K^{(N)}$. Suppose that
$\mathfrak K((s,\cdot),(t,\cdot))$ is continuous on $\mathbb{R}^2$ for every
$s,t\in\mathcal I$, and that, for every finite
$\mathcal A\subset\mathcal I$ and every compact $B\subset\mathbb{R}$,
\[
 \lim_{N\to\infty}
 \max_{s,t\in\mathcal A}\sup_{x,y\in B}
 \left|\mathfrak K^{\left(N\right)}\left(\left(s,x\right),\left(t,y\right)\right)-\mathfrak K\left(\left(s,x\right),\left(t,y\right)\right)\right|=0.
\]
Then $\mathfrak K$ is the extended kernel of a determinantal process
$\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}$, and
\[
    \boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}^{\left(N\right)}\left(\cdot\right)
    \xrightarrow{\mathrm{f.d.d.}}\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}\left(\cdot\right).
\]
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
\label{def al^pm}
For $b>0$, define
    \begin{equation*}
    \begin{aligned}
        \mathbb{W}_b \overset{\mathrm{def}}{=} \left\{\boldsymbol{\alpha}=\left(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\dots\right)\in \left[0,\infty\right)^{\mathbb{N}} :\frac{1}{b}>\alpha_1\geq\alpha_2\geq\dots\geq0, \sum_{i=1}^\infty \alpha_i^2 <\infty\right\}.
    \end{aligned}
    \end{equation*}
We equip $\mathbb{W}_b$ with the metric
\[
 d_{\mathbb W}\left(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\boldsymbol{\beta}\right)
 \overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}2^{-j}
  \min\left\{1,\left|\alpha_j-\beta_j\right|\right\}.
\]
This metric induces coordinatewise convergence. We also define
\[
 s\left(\boldsymbol{\alpha}\right)\overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\alpha_j^2.
\]
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
For $b>0$, define
    \begin{equation*}
    \begin{aligned}
        \mathbb{U}_b \overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}\left\{\mathbf{a}=\left( \left(a_1,a_2,\dots\right),k\right)\in \left[0,\infty\right)^{\mathbb{N}}\times\mathbb{Z}_+ :b>a_1\geq a_2\geq\dots\geq0, \sum_{i=1}^\infty \mathbf{1}_{\left\{a_i>0\right\}}<\infty \right\}.
    \end{aligned}
    \end{equation*}
For $\mathbf a=((a_1,a_2,\ldots),k)\in\mathbb U_b$, define
\[
 m\left(\mathbf a\right)\overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\mathbf{1}_{\left\{a_j>0\right\}},
 \qquad q\left(\mathbf a\right)\overset{\mathrm{def}}{=} m\left(\mathbf a\right)+k.
\]
We equip $\mathbb U_b$ with the metric
\[
 d_{\mathbb U}\left(\mathbf a,\mathbf a'\right)
 \overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}\mathbf{1}_{\left\{q\left(\mathbf a\right)\neq q\left(\mathbf a'\right)\right\}}
  +\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}2^{-j}\min\left\{1,\left|a_j-a'_j\right|\right\}.
\]
Equivalently, $\mathbf a^{(N)}\to\mathbf a$ if its coordinates converge
and $q(\mathbf a^{(N)})=q(\mathbf a)$ for all sufficiently large $N$.
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
\label{def parameter space}
Let $b>0$. Define
\[
\boldsymbol{\Upsilon}_b\overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}\left\{\begin{aligned}
&
\left(\left(\boldsymbol{\alpha}^+,\boldsymbol{\alpha}^-\right),
 \left(\mathbf a^+,\mathbf a^-\right),\gamma_1,\delta\right)
 \in\left(\mathbb W_b\times\mathbb W_b\right)
 \times\left(\mathbb U_b\times\mathbb U_b\right)\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R_+:\\
&\mathbf a^\pm=\left(\left(a_1^\pm,a_2^\pm,\ldots\right),k^\pm\right),\qquad
k^-=0,\qquad
\delta\geq s\left(\boldsymbol{\alpha}^+\right)+s\left(\boldsymbol{\alpha}^-\right)
\end{aligned}\right\}.
\]
We equip $\boldsymbol{\Upsilon}_b$ with the corresponding product topology.
We assign all zero roots to the positive inner coordinate, so $k^-=0$;
this removes the redundancy in the representation of $\mathfrak E_{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}$.
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- definition-10: body_md -->
Let $b>0$ and let $\boldsymbol{\upsilon} = \left((\boldsymbol{\alpha^+},\boldsymbol{\alpha^-}),(\mathbf{a}^+,\mathbf{a}^-),\gamma_1,\delta\right)\in\boldsymbol{\Upsilon}_b$. Denote
    \begin{equation}\label{gamma2}
        \gamma_2=\gamma_2\left(\boldsymbol{\upsilon}\right)
        \overset{\mathrm{def}}{=} \delta-s\left(\boldsymbol{\alpha}^+\right)
                       -s\left(\boldsymbol{\alpha}^-\right)\geq0.
    \end{equation}
    We also define the time horizon
    \[
    \tau\left(\boldsymbol{\upsilon}\right)\overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}
    \begin{cases}
      \gamma_2\left(\boldsymbol{\upsilon}\right)^{-1},&\gamma_2\left(\boldsymbol{\upsilon}\right)>0,\\
      \infty,&\gamma_2\left(\boldsymbol{\upsilon}\right)=0.
    \end{cases}
    \]
    We define $\mathfrak{E}_{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}\colon\mathbb{C}\longrightarrow\mathbb{C},$ as
    \begin{equation}\label{kernel function}
    \begin{aligned}
        \mathfrak{E}_{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}\left(z\right) \overset{\mathrm{def}}{=} {\mathrm{e}}^{-\gamma_1 z-\frac{\gamma_2}{2}z^2}z^{k^++k^-}\prod_{i=1}^{m\left(\mathbf{a}^+\right)}\left(z-a_i^+\right)\prod_{i=1}^{m\left(\mathbf{a}^-\right)}\left(z+a_i^-\right)\prod_{i=1}^\infty {\mathrm{e}}^{z\alpha_i^+} \left(1-z\alpha_i^+\right)\prod_{i=1}^\infty {\mathrm{e}}^{-z\alpha_i^-} \left(1+z\alpha_i^-\right).
    \end{aligned}
    \end{equation}
<!-- end definition-10 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{uniform convergence of entire}
    Let $b>0$ and $({\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}^{(N)})_{N=1}^\infty \subset \boldsymbol{\Upsilon}_b$ be a sequence, and ${\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}\in\boldsymbol{\Upsilon}_b$. If ${\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}^{(N)} \longrightarrow {\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}$, then one has $\mathfrak{E}_{{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}^{(N)}}\longrightarrow\mathfrak{E}_{{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}}$ locally uniformly on $\mathbb{C}$.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
The cited Laguerre--Pólya continuity result gives locally uniform
convergence of the combined Gaussian and genus-product factor under
coordinatewise convergence of $\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{\pm}$ and convergence
of $\gamma_1$ and $\delta$; the individual values $\gamma_2^{(N)}$ need
not converge. For the finite factors, convergence in $\mathbb U_b$ fixes
the total degree
$m(\mathbf a)+k$ eventually. Any positive root which disappears in the
limit converges to zero and is absorbed by the factor $z^k$. Hence
\[
 z^{k^{\left(N\right)}}\prod_{j=1}^{m\left(\mathbf a^{\left(N\right)}\right)}\left(z-a_j^{\left(N\right)}\right)
 \longrightarrow
 z^k\prod_{j=1}^{m\left(\mathbf a\right)}\left(z-a_j\right)
\]
locally uniformly. Applying this separately to the positive and negative
finite factors proves the proposition.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- definition-11: body_md -->
\label{def def of K}
Let $b>0$ and $\boldsymbol{\upsilon}\in\boldsymbol{\Upsilon}_b$. Define
\begin{equation}\label{Gamma}
\begin{aligned}
    &\Gamma_1^+ \overset{\mathrm{def}}{=} \left\{x+ \frac{\mathrm{i}}{\sqrt{3}} x : x \geq \sqrt{3} \right\} \bigcup \left\{x- \frac{\mathrm{i}}{\sqrt{3}} x : x \geq \sqrt{3} \right\},\\
    &\Gamma_1^- \overset{\mathrm{def}}{=} \left\{x+ \frac{\mathrm{i}}{\sqrt{3}} x : x \leq -\sqrt{3} \right\} \bigcup \left\{x- \frac{\mathrm{i}}{\sqrt{3}} x : x \leq -\sqrt{3} \right\},\\
    &\Gamma_2 \overset{\mathrm{def}}{=} \left\{x+\mathrm{i}: -\sqrt{3}\leq x\leq \sqrt{3}\right\}\bigcup\left\{x-\mathrm{i}: -\sqrt{3}\leq x \leq \sqrt{3}\right\},\\ 
    &\Gamma_1 \overset{\mathrm{def}}{=} \Gamma_1^+ \bigcup \Gamma_1^-,\quad\quad \Gamma \overset{\mathrm{def}}{=} \Gamma_1 \bigcup \Gamma_2.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Orient the upper component of $\Gamma$ from $+\infty$ to $-\infty$
and the lower component from $-\infty$ to $+\infty$. For
$L\geq\sqrt{3}$, let $\Gamma_L$ be the positively oriented closed contour
obtained from $\Gamma\cap\{|\Re z|\leq L\}$ by adding the two vertical
end segments. For $w\notin\Gamma$, define
\[
 \operatorname{Ind}_{\Gamma}\left(w\right)
 \overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}\lim_{L\to\infty}\frac{1}{2\pi\mathrm{i}}
   \oint_{\Gamma_L}\frac{\mathrm{d} z}{z-w}.
\]
In particular,
\[
 \operatorname{Ind}_{\Gamma}\left(\mathrm{i} u\right)=\mathbf{1}_{\left\{\left|u\right|<1\right\}}
\]
for Lebesgue-almost every $u\in\mathbb R$.

For $s,t\in(0,\tau(\boldsymbol{\upsilon}))$, $x,y\in\mathbb R$, and an oriented
sub-contour $\Theta\subset\Gamma$, set
\begin{equation}\label{kernel_omega}
\mathfrak A_{\boldsymbol{\upsilon},\Theta}\left(\left(s,x\right),\left(t,y\right)\right)
\overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}\frac{1}{2\pi\mathrm{i}}\int_{\Theta\times\mathbb R}
 \mathfrak h_s\left(x,z\right)\mathfrak h_t\left(-\mathrm{i} y,u\right)
 \frac{1}{\mathrm{i} u-z}
 \frac{\mathfrak E_{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}\left(\mathrm{i} u\right)}{\mathfrak E_{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}\left(z\right)}
 \,\mathrm{d} z\,\mathrm{d} u .
\end{equation}
When $\Theta$ contains either crossing point, this is understood as a
joint two-dimensional improper integral, not as an iterated
principal-value integral. Here
\[
 \mathfrak h_s\left(x,z\right)\overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi s}}
 \mathrm{e}^{-\left(x-z\right)^2/\left(2s\right)}.
\]
Define the parameter-independent residue correction
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathfrak R_{\Gamma}\left(\left(s,x\right),\left(t,y\right)\right)
&\overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}\int_{\mathbb R}\operatorname{Ind}_{\Gamma}\left(\mathrm{i} u\right)
  \mathfrak h_s\left(x,\mathrm{i} u\right)\mathfrak h_t\left(-\mathrm{i} y,u\right)\,\mathrm{d} u\\
&=\int_{-1}^{1}
  \mathfrak h_s\left(x,\mathrm{i} u\right)\mathfrak h_t\left(-\mathrm{i} y,u\right)\,\mathrm{d} u ,
\end{aligned}
\]
the analytic part
\[
 \mathfrak A_{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}\overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}\mathfrak A_{\boldsymbol{\upsilon},\Gamma}+\mathfrak R_{\Gamma},
\]
and the full kernel
\[
 \mathfrak K_{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}\left(\left(s,x\right),\left(t,y\right)\right)
 \overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}\mathfrak A_{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}\left(\left(s,x\right),\left(t,y\right)\right)
  -\mathbf{1}_{\left\{s>t\right\}}\mathfrak h_{s-t}\left(x,y\right).
\]
See Figure~\ref{Gammagraph} for the graph of $\Gamma$.
<!-- end definition-11 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
Below we prove that $\mathfrak K_{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}$ is the kernel of a determinantal process
on $(0,\tau(\boldsymbol{\upsilon}))$ and is obtained as a finite-dimensional Dyson limit.
The estimates establishing convergence of the joint contour integral are
proved in the next section.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- definition-12: body_md -->
\label{reorder xi}
Let $b>0$ and $\boldsymbol{\xi}\in\mathfrak M$ with $\boldsymbol{\xi}(\{0\})=k$ and
$\boldsymbol{\xi}(\{\pm b\})=0$. Put
$m_{\boldsymbol{\xi},b}^+=\boldsymbol{\xi}((0,b))$, $m_{\boldsymbol{\xi},b}^-=\boldsymbol{\xi}((-b,0))$,
$n_{\boldsymbol{\xi},b}^+=\boldsymbol{\xi}((b,\infty))$, and
$n_{\boldsymbol{\xi},b}^-=\boldsymbol{\xi}((-\infty,-b))$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq ordered bxi}
 \boldsymbol{\xi}=k\delta_0+\sum_{i=1}^{m_{\boldsymbol{\xi},b}^+}\delta_{x_{i,<}^+}
 +\sum_{i=1}^{m_{\boldsymbol{\xi},b}^-}\delta_{x_{i,<}^-}
 +\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\boldsymbol{\xi},b}^+}\delta_{x_{i,>}^+}
 +\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\boldsymbol{\xi},b}^-}\delta_{x_{i,>}^-}.
\end{equation}
Order the nonempty particle lists so that
    \begin{equation*}
    \begin{aligned}
        &0<x^+_{m^+_{\boldsymbol{\xi},b},<}\leq \dots\leq x^+_{1,<}<b,\quad
        -b<x^-_{1,<}\leq\dots\leq x^-_{m^-_{\boldsymbol{\xi},b},<}<0,\\
        &b<x^+_{1,>} \leq x_{2,>}^+\leq \dots,\quad -b>x^-_{1,>}\geq x^-_{2,>}\geq \dots.
    \end{aligned}
    \end{equation*}
    We next define
    \begin{equation}\label{M_b}
        \mathfrak{M}_b \overset{\mathrm{def}}{=} \left\{{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\in\mathfrak{M}: {\boldsymbol{\xi}}\left(\left\{\pm b\right\}\right)=0,\quad \sum_{i=1}^{n_{{\boldsymbol{\xi}},b}^+}\left(\frac{1}{x_{i,>}^+}\right)^2 + \sum_{i=1}^{n_{{\boldsymbol{\xi}},b}^-}\left(\frac{1}{x_{i,>}^-}\right)^2 <\infty\right\}. 
    \end{equation}
<!-- end definition-12 -->
<!-- definition-13: body_md -->
For $b>0$ and $r\in\mathbb R$, define the parameter map
    \begin{equation*}
f_r^b\colon\mathfrak{M}_b\longrightarrow\boldsymbol{\Upsilon}_b,\quad {\boldsymbol{\xi}}
    \mapsto \left(\left(\boldsymbol{\alpha^+}\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}\right),\boldsymbol{\alpha^-}\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}\right)\right),
    \left(\mathbf{a}^+\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}\right),\mathbf{a}^-\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}\right)\right),r,\delta\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}\right)\right),
    \end{equation*}
    by
    \begin{equation}\label{eq f_r}
    \begin{aligned}
        &\alpha_j^+\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}\right)\overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}
        \begin{cases}1/x_{j,>}^+,&j\leq n_{\boldsymbol{\xi},b}^+,\\0,&j>n_{\boldsymbol{\xi},b}^+,\end{cases}
        \qquad
        \alpha_j^-\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}\right)\overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}
        \begin{cases}-1/x_{j,>}^-,&j\leq n_{\boldsymbol{\xi},b}^-,\\0,&j>n_{\boldsymbol{\xi},b}^-,\end{cases}\\ 
        &\mathbf{a}^+\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}\right) \overset{\mathrm{def}}{=} \left(\left(x_{1,<}^+,\dots,x_{m_{{\boldsymbol{\xi}},b}^+,<}^+,0,0\dots\right), k\right),\quad \mathbf{a}^-\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}\right) \overset{\mathrm{def}}{=} \left(\left(-x_{1,<}^-,\dots,-x_{m_{{\boldsymbol{\xi}},b}^-,<}^-,0,0,\dots\right), 0\right),\\
        &\gamma_1=r,\quad \delta\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}\right)
        \overset{\mathrm{def}}{=} s\left(\boldsymbol{\alpha}^+\right)+s\left(\boldsymbol{\alpha}^-\right).
    \end{aligned}
    \end{equation}
The dependence of the root coordinates on $b$ is suppressed in the notation.
<!-- end definition-13 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lemma finite contour correction}
Let $\boldsymbol{\xi}$ be a finite configuration with $\boldsymbol{\xi}(\{0\})=0$, choose
$b>0$ with $\boldsymbol{\xi}(\{\pm b\})=0$, and let $C_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}$ be a positively
oriented union of small loops enclosing the support points of $\boldsymbol{\xi}$
and disjoint from $\mathrm{i}\mathbb R$. Products over $a\in\boldsymbol{\xi}$ count
multiplicity. Then, for $s,t>0$ and $x,y\in\mathbb R$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{1}{2\pi\mathrm{i}}
 \int_{C_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\times\mathbb R}
 \mathfrak h_s\left(x,z\right)\mathfrak h_t\left(-\mathrm{i} y,u\right)
 \frac{1}{\mathrm{i} u-z}
 \prod_{a\in\boldsymbol{\xi}}\frac{a-\mathrm{i} u}{a-z}
 \,\mathrm{d} z\,\mathrm{d} u\\
&\hspace{25mm}
=\mathfrak A_{f_{p_b\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}\right)}^b\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}\right),\Gamma}\left(\left(s,x\right),\left(t,y\right)\right)
 +\mathfrak R_{\Gamma}\left(\left(s,x\right),\left(t,y\right)\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
First truncate $\Gamma$ to $\Gamma_L$, with $L$ larger than every
$|a|$, and fix $u$ away from the two crossing values. During the
deformation of $C_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}$ to $\Gamma_L$, the only additional pole is
$z=\mathrm{i} u$. Its residue is
\[
 -\mathfrak h_s\left(x,\mathrm{i} u\right)\mathfrak h_t\left(-\mathrm{i} y,u\right).
\]
The contour $\Gamma_L$ encloses this pole precisely when $|u|<1$.
Thus the residue theorem gives, for the analytic integrand with the
$u$-dependent heat factor included,
\[
 \frac{1}{2\pi\mathrm{i}}\int_{\Gamma_L}\left(\cdots\right)\,\mathrm{d} z
 =\frac{1}{2\pi\mathrm{i}}\int_{C_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}}\left(\cdots\right)\,\mathrm{d} z
  -\mathbf{1}_{\left\{\left|u\right|<1\right\}}
   \mathfrak h_s\left(x,\mathrm{i} u\right)\mathfrak h_t\left(-\mathrm{i} y,u\right).
\]
Rearranging and integrating in $u$ gives the displayed identity.
For a closing segment $z=\pm L+\mathrm{i} v$, $|v|\leq L/\sqrt3$,
\[
 \Re\!\left[-\frac{\left(x-z\right)^2}{2s}\right]
 \leq -\frac{L^2}{3s}+\frac{\left|x\right|L}{s}.
\]
The remaining finite-configuration factors have at most polynomial
growth in $L$ and $u$, whereas $\mathfrak h_t(-\mathrm{i} y,u)$ is Gaussian
in $u$. Consequently the closing-segment integrals vanish as
$L\to\infty$, and dominated convergence yields the integral over
$\Gamma$. The singularities at $(z,u)=(\mathrm{i},1)$ and $(-\mathrm{i},-1)$ are
locally integrable in the joint two-dimensional sense.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{finitedysonmodel}
Let $\boldsymbol{\xi}\in\mathfrak M$ have finite mass $|\boldsymbol{\xi}|$, and choose $b>0$
with $\boldsymbol{\xi}(\{\pm b\})=0$. The $\beta=2$ Dyson Brownian motion started
from $\boldsymbol{\xi}$, understood as its entrance-law extension when $\boldsymbol{\xi}$ has
multiple points, is determinantal at positive times. Its extended kernel
is $\mathfrak K_{f_{p_b(\boldsymbol{\xi})}^b(\boldsymbol{\xi})}$, independently of the admissible choice
of $b$.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
For a simple configuration with no particle at zero,
Proposition~2.1 of \cite{Katori_2009} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq kernel finite dim}
\begin{aligned}
\mathfrak K_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\left(\left(s,x\right),\left(t,y\right)\right)
={}&\frac{1}{2\pi\mathrm{i}}
 \int_{C_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\times\mathbb R}
 \mathfrak h_s\left(x,z\right)\mathfrak h_t\left(-\mathrm{i} y,u\right)
 \frac{1}{\mathrm{i} u-z}
 \prod_{a\in\boldsymbol{\xi}}\frac{a-\mathrm{i} u}{a-z}
 \,\mathrm{d} z\,\mathrm{d} u\\
&-\mathbf{1}_{\left\{s>t\right\}}\mathfrak h_{s-t}\left(x,y\right).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Directly from the definition of $f_{p_b(\boldsymbol{\xi})}^b$,
\[
 \frac{\mathfrak E_{f_{p_b\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}\right)}^b\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}\right)}\left(\mathrm{i} u\right)}
      {\mathfrak E_{f_{p_b\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}\right)}^b\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}\right)}\left(z\right)}
 =\prod_{a\in\boldsymbol{\xi}}\frac{a-\mathrm{i} u}{a-z}.
\]
Lemma~\ref{lemma finite contour correction} identifies
\eqref{eq kernel finite dim} with $\mathfrak K_{f_{p_b(\boldsymbol{\xi})}^b(\boldsymbol{\xi})}$.

For multiple nonzero roots, choose simple real perturbations
$\boldsymbol{\xi}^{(m)}\to\boldsymbol{\xi}$, preserving the number of particles and avoiding
$\{0,\pm b\}$. The finite-particle continuity statement immediately
preceding Proposition~2.1 in \cite{Katori_2009} shows that Dyson
Brownian motion started from $\boldsymbol{\xi}$, including multiplicities, is the
positive-time weak limit of these noncolliding systems. Moreover,
$f_{p_b(\boldsymbol{\xi}^{(m)})}^b(\boldsymbol{\xi}^{(m)})\to
f_{p_b(\boldsymbol{\xi})}^b(\boldsymbol{\xi})$, so Proposition \ref{Uniformconvergence} gives locally uniform convergence of the kernels on each finite set of positive times. Proposition \ref{prop mgf convergence} show that the limiting kernel is determinantal with kernel $\mathfrak K_{f_{p_b(\boldsymbol{\xi})}^b(\boldsymbol{\xi})}$, independently of the chosen perturbation.  Equivalently, the loops in
\eqref{eq kernel finite dim} coalesce into loops around the corresponding
higher-order poles.  If $\boldsymbol{\xi}(\{0\})=k>0$, use distinct positive real
perturbations of the $k$ zero atoms as well; the same argument gives the
shrinking-loop prescription at zero. Finally, the displayed ratio is
intrinsic to $\boldsymbol{\xi}$, so the result does not depend on $b$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{well_defined process}
Let $\boldsymbol{\upsilon}\in\boldsymbol{\Upsilon}_b$. Then $\mathfrak K_{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}$ is the extended kernel of a
determinantal process
$(\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}_{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}(t))_{t\in(0,\tau(\boldsymbol{\upsilon}))}$. Moreover, there
exists a sequence of finite configurations $(\boldsymbol{\xi}^{(n)})_{n\geq1}$
whose $\beta=2$ Dyson models converge to $\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}_{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}$ in
finite-dimensional distributions on every compact subinterval of
$(0,\tau(\boldsymbol{\upsilon}))$.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Write
\[
 \boldsymbol{\upsilon}=\left(\left(\boldsymbol{\alpha}^+,\boldsymbol{\alpha}^-\right),
       \left(\mathbf a^+,\mathbf a^-\right),\gamma_1,\delta\right),
 \qquad k^-=0,
\]
and set
\[
 c_n\overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}\gamma_1-
 \left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}\alpha_j^+
       -\sum_{j=1}^{n}\alpha_j^-\right),
 \qquad
 M_n\overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}\left\lceil n\left(1+\left|c_n\right|+c_n^2\right)\right\rceil,
 \qquad
 v_n\overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}\sqrt{\frac{\gamma_2}{2n}}.
\]
For $a\geq0$ and $m\in\mathbb Z_+$, let $[a]_m$ denote the multiset of
$m$ copies of $a$, with copies of zero omitted. Define finite multisets
\[
\begin{aligned}
 A_n^+
 &\overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}\left\{\alpha_j^+:1\leq j\leq n,\ \alpha_j^+>0\right\}
   \uplus\left[\frac{\max\left(c_n,0\right)}{M_n}\right]_{M_n}
   \uplus\left[v_n\right]_n,\\
 A_n^-
 &\overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}\left\{\alpha_j^-:1\leq j\leq n,\ \alpha_j^->0\right\}
   \uplus\left[\frac{\max\left(-c_n,0\right)}{M_n}\right]_{M_n}
   \uplus\left[v_n\right]_n.
\end{aligned}
\]
Rearrange each multiset in decreasing order. After discarding finitely
many $n$, all its elements lie in $(0,1/b)$. Define
\[
\begin{aligned}
\boldsymbol{\xi}^{\left(n\right)}
\overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}{}&\sum_{j=1}^{m\left(\mathbf a^+\right)}\delta_{a_j^+}
 +\sum_{j=1}^{m\left(\mathbf a^-\right)}\delta_{-a_j^-}
 +\left(k^++k^-\right)\delta_0+\sum_{a\in A_n^+}\delta_{a^{-1}}
 +\sum_{a\in A_n^-}\delta_{-a^{-1}},
\end{aligned}
\]
where multiset elements are counted with multiplicity. The asymmetric
block gives
\[
 \sum_{a\in A_n^+}a-\sum_{a\in A_n^-}a=\gamma_1,
\]
and hence $p_b(\boldsymbol{\xi}^{(n)})=\gamma_1$. Moreover,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \sum_{a\in A_n^+\uplus A_n^-}a^2
={}&\sum_{j=1}^{n}
 \left(\left(\alpha_j^+\right)^2+\left(\alpha_j^-\right)^2\right)
 +\frac{c_n^2}{M_n}+\gamma_2
 \longrightarrow\delta.
\end{aligned}
\]
Indeed,
\[
 \frac{\left|c_n\right|}{M_n}\leq\frac1n,\qquad
 \frac{c_n^2}{M_n}\leq\frac1n,\qquad
 v_n\longrightarrow0.
\]
Set $d_n=\max\{|c_n|/M_n,v_n\}$, so that $d_n\to0$. If
$\alpha_j^\pm>0$, then for all sufficiently large $n$ the added entries
are smaller than $\alpha_j^\pm/2$ and the first $j$ target entries are
present. If $\alpha_j^\pm=0$, the $j$-th rearranged entry is at most
$d_n$. Thus decreasing rearrangement preserves convergence of every
fixed coordinate, and
\[
 \boldsymbol{\upsilon}^{\left(n\right)}
 \overset{\mathrm{def}}{=} f_{p_b\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}^{\left(n\right)}\right)}^b\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}^{\left(n\right)}\right)
 \longrightarrow\boldsymbol{\upsilon}
 \qquad\text{in }\boldsymbol{\Upsilon}_b.
\]
By Proposition~\ref{finitedysonmodel}, $\mathfrak K_{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}^{(n)}}$ is the finite
Dyson kernel. Proposition~\ref{Uniformconvergence}, together with
Proposition~\ref{prop mgf convergence}, yields a determinantal process
with kernel $\mathfrak K_{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}$ and
\[
 \boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}_{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}^{\left(n\right)}}\left(\cdot\right)
 \xrightarrow{\mathrm{f.d.d.}}
 \boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}_{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}\left(\cdot\right)
\]
on $(0,\tau(\boldsymbol{\upsilon}))$, since Proposition~\ref{prop mgf convergence}
applies to every finite set of times in this interval.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{MainTheorem}
Let $b>0$ and suppose that ${\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}^{{(N)}}\longrightarrow\boldsymbol{\upsilon}$ in
$\boldsymbol{\Upsilon}_b$. Put $\tau_N=\tau({\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}^{{(N)}})$ and
$\tau=\tau(\boldsymbol{\upsilon})$. For every finite set $\mathcal A\subset(0,\tau)$ and
every compact set $B\subset\mathbb R$, one has
\begin{equation}\label{eq main local kernel convergence}
 \lim_{N\to\infty}\max_{s,t\in\mathcal A}\sup_{x,y\in B}
 \left|\mathfrak K_{{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}^{{(N)}}}\left(\left(s,x\right),\left(t,y\right)\right)
       -\mathfrak K_{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}\left(\left(s,x\right),\left(t,y\right)\right)\right|=0.
\end{equation}
Moreover, $\mathcal A\subset(0,\tau_N)$ for all sufficiently large $N$.
Consequently, the associated determinantal processes satisfy
\[
 {\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}}^{{(N)}}\left(\cdot\right)
 \xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{f.d.d.}}{\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}}\left(\cdot\right)
 \qquad\hbox{on }\left(0,\tau\right).
\]
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
If $\gamma_2(\boldsymbol{\upsilon})=0$, then $\tau(\boldsymbol{\upsilon})=\infty$, and hence the theorem
holds on every finite time interval.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{bound}
Suppose that ${\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}^{{(N)}}\longrightarrow\boldsymbol{\upsilon}$ in $\boldsymbol{\Upsilon}_b$, and
write $\gamma_2=\gamma_2(\boldsymbol{\upsilon})$. For every $\epsilon>0$ there are
$C_\epsilon<\infty$ and $N_\epsilon\in\mathbb N$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{bdinequality}
\begin{aligned}
 \sup_{N\geq N_\epsilon}\left|\mathfrak E_{{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}^{{(N)}}}\left(z\right)\right|
 &\leq C_\epsilon
       \exp\left(\frac{\gamma_2+\epsilon}{2}\left|z\right|^2\right),
 &&z\in\mathbb C,\\
 \sup_{N\geq N_\epsilon}
 \left|\frac{1}{\mathfrak E_{{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}^{{(N)}}}\left(z\right)}\right|
 &\leq C_\epsilon
       \exp\left(\frac{\gamma_2+\epsilon}{2}\Re\left(z^2\right)\right),
 &&z\in\Gamma .
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The same bounds, after increasing $C_\epsilon$, hold for
$\mathfrak E_{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}$.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lm bound for sum}
For every $\epsilon>0$ there are $N_\epsilon,M_\epsilon\in\mathbb N$
such that
\[
 \sup_{N\geq N_\epsilon}
 \left\{
 \sum_{j=M_\epsilon}^{\infty}\left(\alpha_j^{+,{(N)}}\right)^2+
 \sum_{j=M_\epsilon}^{\infty}\left(\alpha_j^{-,{(N)}}\right)^2+
 \gamma_2^{{(N)}}\right\}
 \leq\gamma_2+\epsilon .
\]
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Choose $M_\epsilon$ so that
\[
 \sum_{j=M_\epsilon}^{\infty}\left(\alpha_j^+\right)^2+
 \sum_{j=M_\epsilon}^{\infty}\left(\alpha_j^-\right)^2\leq\epsilon/2.
\]
For every $N$ the expression inside braces equals
\[
 \delta^{{(N)}}
 -\sum_{j=1}^{M_\epsilon-1}\left(\alpha_j^{+,{(N)}}\right)^2
 -\sum_{j=1}^{M_\epsilon-1}\left(\alpha_j^{-,{(N)}}\right)^2.
\]
Coordinatewise convergence of the displayed finite sums and of
$\delta^{{(N)}}$ makes this at most
\[
 \delta
 -\sum_{j=1}^{M_\epsilon-1}\left(\alpha_j^+\right)^2
 -\sum_{j=1}^{M_\epsilon-1}\left(\alpha_j^-\right)^2+\epsilon/2
 \leq\gamma_2+\epsilon
\]
for all sufficiently large $N$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{denolemma}
If $z\in\mathbb C$ satisfies $|\Re z|=\sqrt3|\Im z|$, then
\[
 \left|\mathrm{e}^z\left(1-z\right)\right|^{-1}\leq
 \exp\left(\frac{\Re\left(z^2\right)}{2}\right).
\]
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
It suffices to write $z=a(1+\mathrm{i}/\sqrt3)$; the other ray is identical.
Then
\[
 \ell\left(a\right)\overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}\log\left|\mathrm{e}^z\left(1-z\right)\right|+\frac{\Re\left(z^2\right)}2
 =a+\frac{a^2}{3}
  +\frac12\log\left(1-2a+\frac43a^2\right)
\]
has derivative
\[
 \ell'\left(a\right)=\frac{8a^3}{3\left(4a^2-6a+3\right)}.
\]
The denominator is strictly positive, so $\ell$ has its global minimum
$\ell(0)=0$ at $a=0$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Apply Lemma~\ref{lm bound for sum} with error $\epsilon/2$, and put
\[
 \mathfrak U_\epsilon^{{(N)}}\left(z\right)\overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}
 \mathrm{e}^{-\gamma_2^{{(N)}}z^2/2}
 \prod_{j=M_{\epsilon/2}}^\infty
 \mathrm{e}^{z\alpha_j^{+,{(N)}}}\left(1-z\alpha_j^{+,{(N)}}\right)
 \mathrm{e}^{-z\alpha_j^{-,{(N)}}}\left(1+z\alpha_j^{-,{(N)}}\right).
\]
By \eqref{naive} and Lemma~\ref{denolemma}, for all sufficiently large $N$,
\[
 \left|\mathfrak U_\epsilon^{{(N)}}\left(z\right)\right|
 \leq\mathrm{e}^{(\gamma_2+\epsilon/2)|z|^2/2}\quad(z\in\mathbb C),\qquad
 \left|\mathfrak U_\epsilon^{{(N)}}\left(z\right)\right|^{-1}
 \leq\mathrm{e}^{(\gamma_2+\epsilon/2)\Re(z^2)/2}\quad(z\in\Gamma_1).
\]
The remaining factor
$\mathfrak E_{{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}^{{(N)}}}/\mathfrak U_\epsilon^{{(N)}}$ has uniformly
bounded polynomial degree, bounded finite-product parameters, and bounded
linear exponential parameter $\gamma_1^{{(N)}}$. Consequently, after
increasing $N_\epsilon$ and changing $C_\epsilon$,
\begin{align}
 \sup_{N\geq N_\epsilon}
 \left|\frac{\mathfrak E_{{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}^{{(N)}}}\left(z\right)}
              {\mathfrak U_\epsilon^{{(N)}}\left(z\right)}\right|
 &\leq C_\epsilon \mathrm{e}^{\epsilon\left|z\right|^2/4},
 &&z\in\mathbb C,\label{eq finite core numerator}\\
 \sup_{N\geq N_\epsilon}
 \left|\frac{\mathfrak U_\epsilon^{{(N)}}\left(z\right)}
              {\mathfrak E_{{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}^{{(N)}}}\left(z\right)}\right|
 &\leq C_\epsilon \mathrm{e}^{\epsilon\Re\left(z^2\right)/4},
 &&z\in\Gamma_1.\label{eq finite core denominator}
\end{align}
Indeed, the polynomial factors have uniformly bounded degree, all
remaining exponential factors have uniformly bounded linear type, and
polynomial and linear-exponential growth can be absorbed into an
arbitrarily small quadratic exponential. On the sloped rays the
finite canonical factors are uniformly separated from zero; for
example,
\[
 \left|1-\alpha a\left(1\pm\mathrm{i}/\sqrt3\right)\right|^2
 =\left(1-\alpha a\right)^2+\frac{\alpha^2a^2}{3}\geq\frac14 .
\]
Equations \eqref{eq finite core numerator} and
\eqref{eq finite core denominator}, with the error split among the
constituent estimates, prove \eqref{bdinequality} on
$\mathbb C$ and $\Gamma_1$. Finally, $\Gamma_2$ is compact and is
disjoint from the real zero set. Proposition
\ref{uniform convergence of entire} therefore gives
\[
 \sup_{N\geq N_\epsilon}\sup_{z\in\Gamma_2}
 \left|\mathfrak E_{{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}^{{(N)}}}\left(z\right)\right|^{-1}<\infty.
\]
The limiting estimates follow in the same way, or by taking limits.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{integralbiliylemma}
For every $L>0$ and $\sigma\in\{-1,1\}$,
\[
 \int_{-\sqrt3}^{\sqrt3}\int_{-L}^{L}
 \frac{\mathrm{d} u\,\mathrm{d} q}{\sqrt{q^2+\left(u-\sigma\right)^2}}<\infty.
\]
More precisely, for $0<\rho<1$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq crossing neighborhood}
 \int_{\left|q\right|<\rho}\int_{\left|u-\sigma\right|<\rho}
 \frac{\mathrm{d} u\,\mathrm{d} q}{\sqrt{q^2+\left(u-\sigma\right)^2}}
 \leq2\pi\sqrt2\,\rho .
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
The integrand is $1/r$ in the two real coordinates
$(q,u-\sigma)$. The square in \eqref{eq crossing neighborhood} is
contained in the disc of radius $\sqrt2\rho$, and polar integration
gives the stated bound. The remainder of the bounded rectangle is
bounded away from the singular point.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{kernel majorant}
Let $0<a<T<\tau(\boldsymbol{\upsilon})$ and let $B\subset\mathbb R$ be compact. Set
$Q=[a,T]^2\times B^2$, and define
\[
 \mathcal J_N\left(s,x,t,y;z,u\right)
 \overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}
 \mathfrak h_s\left(x,z\right)\mathfrak h_t\left(-\mathrm{i} y,u\right)
 \frac{\mathfrak E_{{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}^{{(N)}}}\left(\mathrm{i} u\right)}
      {\left(\mathrm{i} u-z\right)\mathfrak E_{{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}^{{(N)}}}\left(z\right)}.
\]
There exist $c,C>0$ and $N_0\in\mathbb N$ such that, uniformly on $Q$,
for $N\geq N_0$ and
$D\in\{1,\partial_x,\partial_y\}$,
\begin{align}
 \left|D\mathcal J_N\left(s,x,t,y;z,u\right)\right|
 &\leq C\left(1+\left|u\right|+\left|z\right|\right)^2
 \mathrm{e}^{-cu^2-c\left|z\right|^2+C\left|z\right|},
 &&z\in\Gamma_1,\label{eq majorant sloped}\\
 \left|D\mathcal J_N\left(s,x,t,y;q+\mathrm{i}\sigma,u\right)\right|
 &\leq
 \frac{C\left(1+\left|u\right|\right)^2\mathrm{e}^{-cu^2}}
 {\sqrt{q^2+\left(u-\sigma\right)^2}},
 &&q+\mathrm{i}\sigma\in\Gamma_2^\sigma.
 \label{eq majorant crossing}
\end{align}
The same estimates hold for the limiting integrand.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Choose $\epsilon>0$ so small that
$c_0=1/T-\gamma_2-\epsilon>0$, and then use Proposition \ref{bound}.
For the inner heat kernel,
\[
 \left|\mathfrak h_t\left(-\mathrm{i} y,u\right)\right|
 =\left(2\pi t\right)^{-1/2}
 \exp\left(\frac{y^2}{2t}-\frac{u^2}{2t}\right),
\]
and hence its product with
$|\mathfrak E_{{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}^{{(N)}}}(\mathrm{i} u)|$ is bounded by a constant times
$\mathrm{e}^{-c_0u^2/2}$ on $Q$. If
$z=r\pm\mathrm{i} r/\sqrt3\in\Gamma_1$, then
\[
 \Re\left(z^2\right)=\frac23r^2,\qquad
 \left|\mathfrak h_s\left(x,z\right)\right|
 =\left(2\pi s\right)^{-1/2}
 \exp\left(-\frac{x^2-2xr+2r^2/3}{2s}\right).
\]
The reciprocal estimate in \eqref{bdinequality} therefore leaves a
negative quadratic in $r$, uniformly for $(s,x)\in[a,T]\times B$.
Moreover $|\mathrm{i} u-z|\geq|\Re z|=|r|\geq\sqrt3$. This proves
\eqref{eq majorant sloped}. On $\Gamma_2$, compact convergence and
the fact that all zeros are real give a uniform bound for
$|\mathfrak E_{{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}^{{(N)}}}(z)|^{-1}$, while
\[
 \left|\mathrm{i} u-\left(q+\mathrm{i}\sigma\right)\right|=\sqrt{q^2+\left(u-\sigma\right)^2}.
\]
This proves \eqref{eq majorant crossing}. Finally,
\[
 \partial_x\mathfrak h_s\left(x,z\right)
 =-\frac{x-z}{s}\mathfrak h_s\left(x,z\right),\qquad
 \partial_y\mathfrak h_t\left(-\mathrm{i} y,u\right)
 =\frac{y-\mathrm{i} u}{t}\mathfrak h_t\left(-\mathrm{i} y,u\right),
\]
so differentiation contributes only the polynomial factors already
allowed in the two bounds.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{Uniformconvergence}
Let $0<a<T<\tau(\boldsymbol{\upsilon})$ and let $B\subset\mathbb R$ be compact. For
$D\in\{1,\partial_x,\partial_y\}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq uniform analytic convergence}
 \lim_{N\to\infty}
 \sup_{\substack{a\leq s,t\leq T\\x,y\in B}}
 \left|
 D\left\{
 \mathfrak A_{{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}^{{(N)}}}\left(\left(s,x\right),\left(t,y\right)\right)
 -\mathfrak A_{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}\left(\left(s,x\right),\left(t,y\right)\right)
 \right\}\right|=0.
\end{equation}
In particular, for every finite $\mathcal A\subset(0,\tau(\boldsymbol{\upsilon}))$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq uniform full kernel convergence}
 \lim_{N\to\infty}
 \max_{s,t\in\mathcal A}\sup_{x,y\in B}
 \left|
 \mathfrak K_{{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}^{{(N)}}}\left(\left(s,x\right),\left(t,y\right)\right)
 -\mathfrak K_{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}\left(\left(s,x\right),\left(t,y\right)\right)
 \right|=0.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Choose $\epsilon>0$ so that $\gamma_2(\boldsymbol{\upsilon})+\epsilon<1/T$. Lemma
\ref{lm bound for sum} gives
$\gamma_2(\boldsymbol{\upsilon}^{{(N)}})\leq\gamma_2(\boldsymbol{\upsilon})+\epsilon$ for all
sufficiently large $N$. Hence $T<\tau(\boldsymbol{\upsilon}^{{(N)}})$, and the
approximating kernels below are defined on $[a,T]^2\times B^2$ for all
such $N$.
On a compact truncation of $\Gamma\times\mathbb R$ away from the
two crossings, Proposition~\ref{uniform convergence of entire} and
compact convergence of the reciprocals give uniform convergence of
the integrands and their first spatial derivatives, uniformly on
$[a,T]^2\times B^2$. By \eqref{eq majorant crossing} and
\eqref{eq crossing neighborhood}, crossing neighbourhoods of radius
$\rho$ contribute $O(\rho)$ uniformly in $N$ and the external variables.
The tails of the joint integral are uniformly negligible by
\eqref{eq majorant sloped} and the Gaussian factor in
\eqref{eq majorant crossing}. Letting $N\to\infty$, then
$\rho\downarrow0$ and the truncation radius tend to infinity proves
\eqref{eq uniform analytic convergence} for the contour integrals. The residue correction is the same for every $N$, so it
cancels in the displayed difference. The heat-kernel term also
cancels, giving \eqref{eq uniform full kernel convergence}.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
For every finite $\mathcal A\subset(0,\tau(\boldsymbol{\upsilon}))$, Lemma~\ref{lm bound for sum}
gives $\mathcal A\subset(0,\tau_N)$ for all sufficiently large $N$.
Proposition~\ref{Uniformconvergence} proves
\eqref{eq main local kernel convergence}.
Applying Proposition~\ref{prop mgf convergence} on each finite time set
$\mathcal A$ gives the asserted finite-dimensional convergence.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{equivalentkernel}
For a locally bounded determinantal kernel $\mathfrak K$, multiplication by a
gauge factor $\mathfrak g(t,y)/\mathfrak g(s,x)$ leaves every correlation
determinant unchanged: the row and column factors cancel.
Thus the process law is unchanged whenever $\mathfrak g$ and its
reciprocal are measurable and locally bounded.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{gammadependence}
For $0<s,t<\tau_\gamma$,
\begin{equation}\label{Integralterm}
 \mathfrak K_{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}^{\gamma_1,\gamma_2}}
 \left(\left(s,x\right),\left(t,y\right)\right)
 =
 \frac{\mathfrak g\left(t,y\right)}
      {\mathfrak g\left(s,x\right)\sqrt{A_sA_t}}\,
 \mathfrak K_{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}
 \left(\left(\vartheta_{\gamma_2}\left(s\right),\chi_s\left(x\right)\right),
       \left(\vartheta_{\gamma_2}\left(t\right),\chi_t\left(y\right)\right)\right).
\end{equation}
Consequently, if $\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}$ has kernel $\mathfrak K_{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}}$ and
$\Phi_t(q)=A_tq-\gamma_1t$, then
\[
 \boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}^{\gamma_1,\gamma_2}\left(t\right)
 \overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}\left(\Phi_t\right)_\#\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}\left(\vartheta_{\gamma_2}\left(t\right)\right),
 \qquad 0<t<\tau_\gamma,
\]
has kernel $\mathfrak K_{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}^{\gamma_1,\gamma_2}}$.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Completing the two squares gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathfrak h_s\left(x,z\right)\mathrm{e}^{\gamma_1z+\gamma_2z^2/2}
 &=\frac{\mathfrak h_{\vartheta_{\gamma_2}(s)}
            \left(\chi_s\left(x\right),z\right)}
          {\mathfrak g\left(s,x\right)\sqrt{A_s}},\\
 \mathfrak h_t\left(-\mathrm{i} y,u\right)\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma_1\mathrm{i} u+\gamma_2u^2/2}
 &=\frac{\mathfrak g\left(t,y\right)}{\sqrt{A_t}}\,
   \mathfrak h_{\vartheta_{\gamma_2}(t)}
            \left(-\mathrm{i}\chi_t\left(y\right),u\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
Substituting in \eqref{kernel_omega} proves \eqref{Integralterm} for
the contour integrals. At $z=\mathrm{i} u$ the parameter-dependent
exponentials cancel, so the same identities give
\[
 \mathfrak R_\Gamma\left(\left(s,x\right),\left(t,y\right)\right)
 =
 \frac{\mathfrak g\left(t,y\right)}
      {\mathfrak g\left(s,x\right)\sqrt{A_sA_t}}\,
 \mathfrak R_\Gamma\left(
  \left(\vartheta_{\gamma_2}\left(s\right),\chi_s\left(x\right)\right),
  \left(\vartheta_{\gamma_2}\left(t\right),\chi_t\left(y\right)\right)\right).
\]
Thus the analytic parts obey the same identity. For $s>t$,
a further completion of squares gives
\begin{equation}\label{heatkernelterm}
 \mathfrak h_{s-t}\left(x,y\right)
 =
 \frac{\mathfrak g\left(t,y\right)}
      {\mathfrak g\left(s,x\right)\sqrt{A_sA_t}}\,
 \mathfrak h_{\vartheta_{\gamma_2}(s)-\vartheta_{\gamma_2}(t)}
       \left(\chi_s\left(x\right),\chi_t\left(y\right)\right).
\end{equation}
Since $\vartheta_{\gamma_2}$ is strictly increasing, the time-order
indicator is unchanged. Subtracting \eqref{heatkernelterm} proves
\eqref{Integralterm}.

The change of variables $x=\Phi_t(q)$ gives the spatial Jacobian
$1/\sqrt{A_sA_t}$ in the transformed kernel. The remaining factor
is removed by Remark~\ref{equivalentkernel}, proving the process statement.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{prop:gamma2-horizon-sharpness}
Fix $\gamma>0$ and set
\[
 t_c\overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}\gamma^{-1},\qquad
 a_N\overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}\sqrt{2N/\gamma},\qquad
 \boldsymbol{\xi}^{(N)}\overset{\mathrm{def}}{=} N\left(\delta_{a_N}+\delta_{-a_N}\right).
\]
For any fixed $b>0$, the parameters $f_0^b(\boldsymbol{\xi}^{(N)})$, defined for all
sufficiently large $N$, converge to a parameter $\boldsymbol{\upsilon}_\gamma$ with
$\gamma_2(\boldsymbol{\upsilon}_\gamma)=\gamma$. Let $\rho_t^{(N)}$ be the first correlation
function of the $\beta=2$ Dyson Brownian motion from $\boldsymbol{\xi}^{(N)}$, in the
entrance-law sense of Proposition~\ref{finitedysonmodel}. Then
\[
 \rho_{t_c}^{\left(N\right)}\left(0\right)
 \sim\frac{\Gamma\left(3/4\right)\sqrt\gamma}
 {2^{1/4}\pi^{3/2}}N^{1/4},\qquad
 \rho_t^{\left(N\right)}\left(0\right)
 \sim\frac{a_N}{\pi t}\sqrt{\gamma t-1}\quad\left(t>t_c\right),
\]
where $\Gamma$ denotes Euler's gamma function. In particular, the first
correlation functions cannot converge locally uniformly to a finite
function at any fixed $t\geq t_c$.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
For large $N$, all roots lie outside $[-b,b]$. Both reciprocal sequences
consist of $N$ copies of $a_N^{-1}$ followed by zeros, and their combined
square sum is $2N/a_N^2=\gamma$. The reciprocal sum is zero and the inner
root data are empty. Thus the parameters converge coordinatewise with
$\gamma_1=0$, $\delta=\gamma$ and both limiting reciprocal sequences zero.
This gives $\gamma_2(\boldsymbol{\upsilon}_\gamma)=\gamma$.

We first compute the density for the finite cloud
$N(\delta_a+\delta_{-a})$, with arbitrary $a,t>0$. Write it as
$\rho_t^{N,a}$ and let $\mathsf G_N$ be a sum of $N$ independent
exponential random variables of mean one. We claim that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gamma2-gamma-density}
 \rho_t^{N,a}\left(0\right)
 =\frac{1}{\pi t}\mathbb{E}\left[
       \left(2t\mathsf G_N-a^2\right)_+^{1/2}\right].
\end{equation}
Here $q_+=\max\{q,0\}$. To prove the identity, take a positively oriented
small circle $D$ about $a^2$, disjoint from $(-\infty,0]$, and let $C$ be
its two inverse images under $z\mapsto z^2$. The finite kernel formula
\eqref{eq kernel finite dim}, at $s=t$ and $x=y=0$, gives
\[
 \rho_t^{N,a}\left(0\right)
 =\frac{1}{2\pi t}\int_{\mathbb R}\mathrm{e}^{-u^2/\left(2t\right)}
 \frac{1}{2\pi\mathrm{i}}\oint_C
 \frac{\mathrm{e}^{-z^2/\left(2t\right)}}{\mathrm{i} u-z}
 \left(\frac{a^2+u^2}{a^2-z^2}\right)^N\,\mathrm{d} z\,\mathrm{d} u.
\]
These integrals are absolutely convergent. Averaging the integrand over
$u$ and $-u$ replaces $(\mathrm{i} u-z)^{-1}$ by $-z/(z^2+u^2)$.
Set $c=a^2+u^2$ and change variables to $w=z^2$ on each component of
$C$. The two Jacobian factors of $1/2$ add, and expansion at $w=a^2$
evaluates the resulting contour integral as
\[
 -\frac{c^N}{2\pi\mathrm{i}}\oint_D
 \frac{\mathrm{e}^{-w/\left(2t\right)}}{\left(a^2-w\right)^N\left(w+u^2\right)}\,\mathrm{d} w
 =\mathrm{e}^{-a^2/\left(2t\right)}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\frac{\left(c/\left(2t\right)\right)^k}{k!}.
\]
Since $\mathbb{P}(\mathsf G_N>v)=\mathrm{e}^{-v}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}v^k/k!$ for $v\geq0$,
Tonelli's theorem now gives
\[
 \rho_t^{N,a}\left(0\right)
 =\frac{1}{2\pi t}\int_{\mathbb R}
   \mathbb{P}\left(2t\mathsf G_N>a^2+u^2\right)\,\mathrm{d} u
 =\frac{1}{\pi t}\mathbb{E}\left[
   \left(2t\mathsf G_N-a^2\right)_+^{1/2}\right].
\]

For $a=a_N$ and $t>t_c$, divide \eqref{eq:gamma2-gamma-density} by
$\sqrt N$. Since $\mathsf G_N/N\to1$ in $L^2$ and
$|\sqrt{x_+}-\sqrt{y_+}|\leq\sqrt{|x-y|}$,
\[
 \frac{\rho_t^{\left(N\right)}\left(0\right)}{\sqrt N}
 \longrightarrow\frac{\sqrt{2t-2/\gamma}}{\pi t}.
\]
At $t=t_c$, put $\mathsf Z_N=(\mathsf G_N-N)/\sqrt N$. The central limit
theorem gives $\mathsf Z_N\xrightarrow{\mathrm{law}}\mathsf Z$, where $\mathsf Z$ is
standard normal. Moreover,
$\mathbb{E}[(\mathsf Z_N)_+^2]\leq\mathbb{E}[\mathsf Z_N^2]=1$, so
$((\mathsf Z_N)_+^{1/2})_{N\geq1}$ is uniformly integrable. Therefore
\[
 \frac{\rho_{t_c}^{\left(N\right)}\left(0\right)}{N^{1/4}}
 =\frac{\sqrt{2\gamma}}{\pi}
      \mathbb{E}\left[\left(\mathsf Z_N\right)_+^{1/2}\right]
 \longrightarrow\frac{\sqrt{2\gamma}}{\pi\sqrt{2\pi}}
       \int_0^\infty v^{1/2}\mathrm{e}^{-v^2/2}\,\mathrm{d} v
 =\frac{\Gamma\left(3/4\right)\sqrt\gamma}{2^{1/4}\pi^{3/2}}.\qedhere
\]
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{theorem path cts}
 Let \(b>0\), let \(\boldsymbol{\xi}^{(N)}\in\mathfrak{M}^0\cap\mathfrak{M}_b\),
 and let \(r^{(N)}\to r\).  Put
 \[
       \boldsymbol{\upsilon}^{(N)}\overset{\mathrm{def}}{=} f_{r^{(N)}}^b\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}^{(N)}\right),
 \]
 and assume that
 \[
       \boldsymbol{\upsilon}^{(N)}\longrightarrow\boldsymbol{\upsilon}\quad\hbox{in }\boldsymbol{\Upsilon}_b.
 \]
 Write
 \(\mathbf a^\pm=((a_i^\pm)_{i\geq1},k^\pm)\), and let \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) be the
 root configuration encoded by \(\boldsymbol{\upsilon}\), namely
 \[
 \boldsymbol{\xi}\overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}\left(k^++k^-\right)\delta_0
      +\sum_{i=1}^{m\left(\mathbf a^+\right)}\delta_{a_i^+}
      +\sum_{i=1}^{m\left(\mathbf a^-\right)}\delta_{-a_i^-}
      +\sum_{\alpha_i^+>0}\delta_{1/\alpha_i^+}
      +\sum_{\alpha_i^->0}\delta_{-1/\alpha_i^-}.
 \]
 Assume that \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) is simple and infinite, and that there is a decreasing function
 \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{sep}}\colon[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)\), with
 \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{sep}}(R)\to0\), such that
 \begin{equation}\label{extra condition}
  \text{for every \(N\) and every \(x\in\boldsymbol{\xi}^{(N)}\),}\qquad
  \sum_{\substack{y\in\boldsymbol{\xi}^{(N)}\\y\ne x,\,-x}}
       \frac1{\left|y^2-x^2\right|}
  \leq \varepsilon_{\mathrm{sep}}\left(\left|x\right|\right).
 \end{equation}
 Let \(\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}^{(N)}\) be the process with kernel
 \(\mathfrak K_{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}^{(N)}}\).  Then
 \[
     \boldsymbol{\upsilon}=f_r^b\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}\right),
 \]
 the processes \(\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}^{(N)}\) and the process
 \(\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}\) with kernel \(\mathfrak K_{f_r^b(\boldsymbol{\xi})}\) have continuous
 versions on \([0,\infty)\), with
 \(\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}^{(N)}(0)=\boldsymbol{\xi}^{(N)}\) and
 \(\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}(0)=\boldsymbol{\xi}\), and
 \begin{equation*}
   \boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}^{(N)}\left(\cdot\right)
   \xrightarrow{\mathrm{law}}
   \boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}\left(\cdot\right)
   \quad\text{in }\mathcal C\left(\left[0,\infty\right)\to\mathfrak M\right).
 \end{equation*}
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{gamma_2 is 0}
 Under the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{theorem path cts},
 $\gamma_2(\boldsymbol{\upsilon})=0$ and hence $\boldsymbol{\upsilon}=f_r^b(\boldsymbol{\xi})$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Parameter convergence implies rootwise convergence of $\boldsymbol{\xi}^{(N)}$ to $\boldsymbol{\xi}$.
Indeed, eventual equality of $q(\mathbf a)=m(\mathbf a)+k$ and coordinate convergence in
$\mathbb U_b$ match the finite inner multisets, including roots absorbed
at zero. Outside $[-b,b]$, the decreasing reciprocal coordinates match
the finitely many entries exceeding $1/R$ whenever
$\boldsymbol{\xi}(\{\pm R\})=0$; their number is eventually constant. Restricting the
inner matching when $R\leq b$, and combining these matchings when $R>b$,
gives the required bijections. The $\gamma_1$-coordinate of $\boldsymbol{\upsilon}$ is
$r$, so only the equality of its square coordinate with the root square
mass remains to be proved. Write $\gamma_2=\gamma_2(\boldsymbol{\upsilon})$.
 For every \(N\),
 \[
  \delta^{(N)}
   =s\left(\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{+,{(N)}}\right)
     +s\left(\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{-,{(N)}}\right)
   =\sum_{\substack{y\in\boldsymbol{\xi}^{(N)}\\\left|y\right|>b}}\frac1{y^2}.
 \]
 Choose \(L>b\) outside the countable set
 \(\{|x|:x\in\operatorname{supp}(\boldsymbol{\xi})
          \cup\bigcup_N\operatorname{supp}(\boldsymbol{\xi}^{(N)})\}\).
 Rootwise convergence on the compact annulus
 \(\{b<|y|<L\}\), together with \(\delta^{(N)}\to\delta\), gives
 \begin{equation}\label{escaped square mass}
 \begin{aligned}
  \lim_{N\to\infty}
  \sum_{\substack{y\in\boldsymbol{\xi}^{(N)}\\\left|y\right|\geq L}}\frac1{y^2}
   &=\delta-
     \sum_{\substack{y\in\boldsymbol{\xi}\\b<\left|y\right|<L}}\frac1{y^2}=\gamma _2+
     \sum_{\substack{y\in\boldsymbol{\xi}\\\left|y\right|\geq L}}\frac1{y^2}
   \geq\gamma _2 .
 \end{aligned}
 \end{equation}

 Suppose that \(\gamma _2>0\).  Since \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) is infinite and locally
 finite, choose \(x\in\boldsymbol{\xi}\) so far from the origin that
 \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{sep}}(|x|/2)<\gamma _2/2\), and let
 \(x^{(N)}\in\boldsymbol{\xi}^{(N)}\) be its matched atom.  Next choose \(L\), as above,
 with \(L>2\sup_{N\geq N_0}|x^{(N)}|\).  For all sufficiently large \(N\),
 every atom \(y\) in the sum below is different from \(x^{(N)}\) and
 \(-x^{(N)}\), and
 \[
  \sum_{\substack{y\in\boldsymbol{\xi}^{(N)}\\\left|y\right|\geq L}}\frac1{y^2}
  \leq
  \sum_{\substack{y\in\boldsymbol{\xi}^{(N)}\\\left|y\right|\geq L}}
       \frac1{\left|y^2-\left(x^{(N)}\right)^2\right|}
  \leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{sep}}\left(\left|x^{(N)}\right|\right)
  \leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{sep}}\left(\left|x\right|/2\right)<\frac{\gamma _2}{2}.
 \]
 This contradicts \eqref{escaped square mass}.  Hence \(\gamma _2=0\).
 Therefore \(\boldsymbol{\upsilon}=f_r^b(\boldsymbol{\xi})\).
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- definition-14: body_md -->
\label{residue function}
 For \(r\in\mathbb R\), \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\in\mathfrak M_b\cap\mathfrak M^0\),
 \(x\in\boldsymbol{\xi}\), and \(z\in\mathbb C\), define
 \begin{equation*}
 \mathfrak F_{\boldsymbol{\xi},r}\left(x,z\right)\overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}
 \frac{\mathfrak E_{f_r^b\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}\setminus\left\{x\right\}\right)}\left(z\right)}
      {\mathfrak E_{f_r^b\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}\setminus\left\{x\right\}\right)}\left(x\right)}
 \begin{cases}
  1,& \left|x\right|<b,\\
  \exp\left(z/x-1\right),& \left|x\right|>b.
 \end{cases}
 \end{equation*}
 Since \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) is simple, the denominator is nonzero.
<!-- end definition-14 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{bound of res}
 Under the assumptions of Theorem \ref{theorem path cts}, for every
 \(\eta>0\) there is a finite \(C_\eta\), independent of \(N,L,x,z\),
 such that
 \begin{equation}\label{eq bound of res}
 \left|\mathfrak F_{\boldsymbol\zeta,r_*}\left(x,z\right)\right|
 \leq C_\eta\exp\left(\eta\left(|x|^2+|z|^2\right)\right),
 \qquad x\in\boldsymbol\zeta,\quad z\in\mathbb C,
 \end{equation}
 for each of the pairs
 $(\boldsymbol\zeta,r_*)=(\boldsymbol{\xi}^{(N)},r^{(N)})$,
 $(\boldsymbol{\xi}^{{(N)},[L]},r^{(N)})$, $(\boldsymbol{\xi},r)$, and $(\boldsymbol{\xi}^{[L]},r)$.
 Moreover, if
 \(x^{(N)}\to x\) are matched roots, then
 \begin{equation}\label{residue local convergence}
  \mathfrak F_{\boldsymbol{\xi}^{(N)},r^{(N)}}\left(x^{(N)},\cdot\right)
   \longrightarrow\mathfrak F_{\boldsymbol{\xi},r}\left(x,\cdot\right)
 \end{equation}
 locally uniformly on \(\mathbb C\).  The analogous assertion holds as
 \(L\to\infty\) for spatial truncations.
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Lemma \ref{gamma_2 is 0}, coordinatewise convergence, and convergence of
 the \(\delta\)-coordinates imply the uniform square-tail estimate
 \begin{equation}\label{uniform square tail}
  \lim_{M\to\infty}\ \sup_N
  \left\{\sum_{j\geq M}\left(\alpha_j^{+,{(N)}}\right)^2+
         \sum_{j\geq M}\left(\alpha_j^{-,{(N)}}\right)^2\right\}=0.
 \end{equation}
 Indeed, subtract the first \(M-1\) convergent square coordinates from
 \(\delta^{(N)}\to
 s(\boldsymbol{\alpha}^+)+s(\boldsymbol{\alpha}^-)\).
 Deleting roots only decreases the left hand side.  The canonical-product
 inequality
 \[
       \left|\left(1-w\right)\mathrm{e}^w\right|\leq \mathrm{e}^{\left|w\right|^2/2}
 \]
 applied after separating finitely many root coordinates therefore yields,
 uniformly for \(\boldsymbol{\zeta}\) equal to any of
 \(\boldsymbol{\xi}^{(N)},\boldsymbol{\xi}^{{(N)},[L]},\boldsymbol{\xi},\boldsymbol{\xi}^{[L]}\),
 \begin{equation}\label{residue numerator bound}
  \left|\mathfrak E_{f_{r_*}^b\left(\boldsymbol{\zeta}\setminus\left\{x\right\}\right)}\left(z\right)\right|
   \leq C_\eta \mathrm{e}^{\eta\left|z\right|^2},
 \end{equation}
 where \(r_*=r^{(N)}\) or \(r\), respectively.  Here the bounded
 \(r_*\)'s and the uniformly finite collection of roots in a compact
 interval are absorbed into \(C_\eta\).

 We spell out the denominator estimate, since it is where
 \eqref{extra condition} is needed.  For \(x^2\ne y^2\) and $y\neq0$,
 \begin{equation}\label{simple equality}
  \frac1{\left(1-x/y\right)\mathrm{e}^{x/y}}
  =\left(1+\frac{x^2}{y^2-x^2}\right)
    \left(1+x/y\right)\mathrm{e}^{-x/y}.
 \end{equation}
 Put
 \[
  I_{\boldsymbol\zeta,x}
    \overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}\left\{y\in\boldsymbol\zeta\setminus\left\{x\right\}:\left|y\right|<b\right\},
  \qquad
  O_{\boldsymbol\zeta,x}
    \overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}\left\{y\in\boldsymbol\zeta\setminus\left\{x\right\}:\left|y\right|>b\right\}.
 \]
 Since configurations in \(\mathfrak M_b\) have no roots at \(\pm b\),
 the definition of the canonical product gives the exact factorization
 \begin{equation}\label{denominator core split}
 \begin{aligned}
 &\left|
  \mathfrak E_{f_{r_*}^b\left(\boldsymbol\zeta\setminus\left\{x\right\}\right)}\left(x\right)
  \right|^{-1}={\mathrm{e}}^{r_* x}
  \prod_{y\in I_{\boldsymbol\zeta,x}}\left|x-y\right|^{-1}
  \prod_{y\in O_{\boldsymbol\zeta,x}}
       \left|\left(1-x/y\right)\mathrm{e}^{x/y}\right|^{-1}.
 \end{aligned}
 \end{equation}
 The number of inner roots is uniformly bounded.  If \(|x|\geq2b\),
 then \(|x-y|\geq|x|/2\) for every inner root.  If \(|x|<2b\),
 rootwise convergence to the simple limiting configuration makes the
 distinct roots in a fixed larger compact interval uniformly separated;
 the finitely many exceptional \(N\)'s are absorbed into the constant.
 The same statement holds for the truncations, which contain the same
 inner core.  Consequently, for every \(\eta>0\),
 \begin{equation}\label{inner core bound}
  \prod_{y\in I_{\boldsymbol\zeta,x}}\left|x-y\right|^{-1}
  \leq C_\eta \mathrm{e}^{\eta x^2}
 \end{equation}
 uniformly over the four families of configurations under consideration.

 Apply \eqref{simple equality} only to the outer roots.  If
 \(-x\in O_{\boldsymbol\zeta,x}\), then necessarily \(|x|>b\), and that
 one outer canonical factor contributes exactly \(\mathrm{e}/2\) to the inverse.
 For all remaining outer roots, the product of the final factors in
 \eqref{simple equality}, together with \(\mathrm{e}^{r_* x}\), is the canonical
 product at \(x\) of the reflected outer subconfiguration, with parameter
 \(-r_*\).  The proof of \eqref{residue numerator bound} applies to this
 product: reflection preserves square tails, deletion decreases them,
 and \(-r_*\) remains bounded.  Hence its absolute value is at most
 \(C_\eta \mathrm{e}^{\eta x^2}\).  Finally, using
 \(|1+a|\leq \mathrm{e}^{|a|}\), with \(a=x^2/(y^2-x^2)\), in
 \eqref{denominator core split}, and shrinking \(\eta\) at the start,
 gives
 \begin{equation}\label{residue denominator bound}
 \left|
  \mathfrak E_{f_{r_*}^b\left(\boldsymbol{\zeta}\setminus\left\{x\right\}\right)}\left(x\right)
 \right|^{-1}
 \leq C_\eta \mathrm{e}^{\eta x^2}
 \exp\left\{
   x^2\sum_{\substack{y\in\boldsymbol{\zeta}\\y\ne x,-x}}
          \frac1{\left|y^2-x^2\right|}
 \right\}.
 \end{equation}
 Truncation decreases the sum.  For \(\boldsymbol{\zeta}=\boldsymbol{\xi}^{(N)}\),
 \eqref{extra condition} bounds it by
 \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{sep}}(|x|)\); for the limiting configuration, Fatou's
 lemma gives the same conclusion with
 \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{sep}}(|x|/2)\).  Since this tends to zero, its product
 with \(x^2\) is absorbed into \(\mathrm{e}^{\eta x^2}\) for large \(|x|\), while
 bounded \(x\)'s are absorbed into \(C_\eta\).
 The extra factor \(\exp(z/x-1)\), when present, is also absorbed by
 \(2|z/x|\leq\eta|z|^2+\eta^{-1}x^{-2}\) and \(|x|>b\).
 Combining \eqref{residue numerator bound} and
 \eqref{residue denominator bound}, and replacing \(\eta\) by a smaller
 number at the start, proves \eqref{eq bound of res}.

 Finally, deleting a matched root from the parameter tuple preserves
 coordinatewise convergence (and changes the square coordinate by the
 corresponding reciprocal square when the root lies outside \([-b,b]\)).
 Proposition \ref{uniform convergence of entire}, together with the
 nonvanishing of the limiting denominator, then proves
 \eqref{residue local convergence}.  The proof for truncations is
 identical.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{theorem complex repre}
 Fix \(b>0\), let
 \(\boldsymbol{\eta}\in\mathfrak M_b\) be finite and simple, let
 \(r\in\mathbb R\), and let \(T>0\). If \(G\) is a bounded
 cylinder functional of the configuration path up to time \(T\), then
 \begin{equation}\label{finite arbitrary r representation}
 \mathbb{E}_{r,\boldsymbol{\eta}}^{\mathrm{DBM}}\left[G\left(\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}\right)\right]
 =
 \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}}^{\mathrm{BM}}\left[
  G\left(\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{\mathsf X_i\left(\cdot\right)}\right)
  \det\left[
    \mathfrak F_{\boldsymbol{\eta},r}\left(x_i,\mathsf Z_j\left(T\right)\right)
  \right]_{i,j=1}^n
 \right].
 \end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Directly from Definition \ref{residue function},
 \begin{equation}\label{finite bridge factor}
  \mathfrak F_{\boldsymbol{\eta},r}\left(x,z\right)
   =\exp\left\{-\left(r-p_b\left(\boldsymbol{\eta}\right)\right)\left(z-x\right)\right\}
     \mathfrak P_{\boldsymbol{\eta}}^x\left(z\right).
 \end{equation}
 Put \(c=r-p_b(\boldsymbol{\eta})\).  The standard finite Dyson
 representation (the case \(c=0\)) is the determinantal-martingale
 representation of \cite{MR3019667}.  Factoring the exponential in
 \eqref{finite bridge factor} out of rows and columns gives
 \[
 \det\left[\mathfrak F_{\boldsymbol{\eta},r}\left(x_i,\mathsf Z_j\left(T\right)\right)\right]
 =
 \mathrm{e}^{-c\sum_j\left(\mathsf Z_j\left(T\right)-x_j\right)}
 \det\left[\mathfrak P_{\boldsymbol{\eta}}^{x_i}\left(\mathsf Z_j\left(T\right)\right)\right].
 \]
 For independent standard real Brownian motions \(\mathsf B,\mathsf Y\)
 and a polynomial \(H\), Gaussian integration gives
 \[
 \begin{aligned}
  \mathbb{E}\left[\mathrm{e}^{-c\mathsf B\left(T\right)}F\left(\mathsf B\right)\right]
    &=\mathrm{e}^{c^2T/2}\mathbb{E}\left[F\left(\mathsf B-c\,\cdot\right)\right],\\
  \mathbb{E}\left[\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i} c\mathsf Y\left(T\right)}H\left(a+\mathrm{i} \mathsf Y\left(T\right)\right)\right]
    &=\mathrm{e}^{-c^2T/2}\mathbb{E}\left[H\left(a+cT+\mathrm{i} \mathsf Y\left(T\right)\right)\right].
 \end{aligned}
 \]
 The first identity is Cameron--Martin and the second is the elementary
 Gaussian contour shift, justified here because the determinant is a
 polynomial in each complex endpoint.  The scalar factors cancel.  The
 real shift sends \(\mathsf X_j(t)\) to \(\mathsf X_j(t)-ct\), while the \(+cT\) in the
 imaginary identity cancels that shift inside
 \(\mathsf Z_j(T)=\mathsf X_j(T)+\mathrm{i} \mathsf Y_j(T)\).  Hence
 \begin{align*}
 &\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}}\left[
  G\left(\sum_i\delta_{\mathsf X_i\left(\cdot\right)}\right)
  \mathrm{e}^{-c\sum_j\left(\mathsf Z_j\left(T\right)-x_j\right)}
  \det\left[\mathfrak P_{\boldsymbol{\eta}}^{x_i}\left(\mathsf Z_j\left(T\right)\right)\right]
 \right]=
 \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}}\left[
  G\left(\sum_i\delta_{\mathsf X_i\left(\cdot\right)-ct}\right)
  \det\left[\mathfrak P_{\boldsymbol{\eta}}^{x_i}\left(\mathsf Z_j\left(T\right)\right)\right]
 \right].
 \end{align*}
 This identity follows first for bounded cylinder functions by ordinary
 Gaussian integration and then by a monotone-class argument.  By
 Proposition \ref{gammadependence}, changing the \(\gamma _1\)-coordinate
 from \(p_b(\boldsymbol{\eta})\) to \(r\) shifts every particle by
 \(-ct=-(r-p_b(\boldsymbol{\eta}))t\).  Applying the standard representation proves
 \eqref{finite arbitrary r representation}.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- cor-1: body_md -->
\label{complex representation}
Let $\phi\in\mathcal C_c^1(\mathbb R)$, $0\leq s<t\leq T$, and $Q\in\mathbb N$.
Then
 \begin{equation}\label{eq complex representation}
 \begin{aligned}
 &\mathbb{E}_{r,\boldsymbol{\eta}}
 \left[
  \left\{\left\langle\phi,\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}\left(t\right)\right\rangle
    -\left\langle\phi,\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}\left(s\right)\right\rangle\right\}^{Q}
 \right]
 =
 \sum_{q=1}^{Q}
 \sum_{\substack{p_1,\ldots,p_q\geq1\\p_1+\cdots+p_q=Q}}
 \binom{Q}{p_1,\ldots,p_q}\\
 &\qquad\times
 \sum_{\substack{x_{i_1}>\cdots>x_{i_q}\\x_{i_j}\in\boldsymbol{\eta}}}
 \mathbb{E}\left[
  \prod_{j=1}^q
   \left\{\phi\left(\mathsf X_{i_j}\left(t\right)\right)-\phi\left(\mathsf X_{i_j}\left(s\right)\right)\right\}^{p_j}
  \det\left[
   \mathfrak F_{\boldsymbol{\eta},r}
      \left(x_{i_j},\mathsf Z_{i_k}\left(T\right)\right)
  \right]_{j,k=1}^q
 \right].
 \end{aligned}
 \end{equation}
<!-- end cor-1 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Expand the $Q$-th power in \eqref{finite arbitrary r representation} and
group terms by their distinct particle indices and multiplicities.
For an unused index $j$, independence and the complex Brownian
martingale identity give
\[
 \mathbb{E}\left[\mathfrak F_{\boldsymbol\eta,r}
                  \left(x_i,\mathsf Z_j\left(T\right)\right)\right]
 =\mathfrak F_{\boldsymbol\eta,r}\left(x_i,x_j\right)=\delta_{ij}.
\]
The identity is applicable because \eqref{finite bridge factor} is an
exponential times a polynomial. Integrating each unused column therefore
removes its corresponding row and column, yielding
\eqref{eq complex representation}, also when $s=0$.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lemma for bound}
 Let \(\mathcal A\subset(\mathfrak M_b\cap\mathfrak M^0)\times\mathbb R\)
 be a family of pairs \((\boldsymbol\zeta,r)\) for which the residue estimate
 \eqref{eq bound of res} holds with common constants and
 \begin{equation}\label{uniform gaussian summability}
   \sup_{(\boldsymbol{\zeta},r)\in\mathcal A}
   \sum_{x\in\boldsymbol{\zeta}}\mathrm{e}^{-c x^2}<\infty
   \qquad\text{for every }c>0.
 \end{equation}
 For every even \(Q\geq4\), \(T<\infty\), and
 \(\phi\in\mathcal C_c^1(\mathbb R)\), there is
 \(C_{Q,T,\phi}<\infty\) such that, for every
 \((\boldsymbol\zeta,r)\in\mathcal A\) with \(\boldsymbol\zeta\) finite,
 and \(0\leq s,t\leq T\),
 \begin{equation}\label{even Q moment estimate}
 \mathbb{E}_{r,\boldsymbol{\zeta}}\left[
 \left|
  \left\langle\phi,\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}\left(t\right)\right\rangle
  -\left\langle\phi,\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}\left(s\right)\right\rangle
 \right|^Q\right]
 \leq C_{Q,T,\phi}\left|t-s\right|^{Q/2}.
 \end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Fix a term in \eqref{eq complex representation}, with
 \(p_1+\cdots+p_q=Q\), and let \(K=\operatorname{supp}\phi\).  Put
 \[
  \mathsf I_j\overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}\mathbf{1}\left\{\mathsf X_{i_j}\left(s\right)\in K
                      \text{ or }\mathsf X_{i_j}\left(t\right)\in K\right\}.
 \]
 The corresponding difference of \(\phi\)'s vanishes unless \(\mathsf I_j=1\),
 and the mean-value theorem gives
 \[
 \left|\phi\left(\mathsf X_{i_j}\left(t\right)\right)-\phi\left(\mathsf X_{i_j}\left(s\right)\right)\right|^{p_j}
 \leq \left\|\phi'\right\|_\infty^{p_j}
      \left|\mathsf X_{i_j}\left(t\right)-\mathsf X_{i_j}\left(s\right)\right|^{p_j}\mathsf I_j .
 \]
 Hölder's inequality with exponents \(2,4,4\) bounds the absolute value
 of the expectation in this term by
 \begin{align}
 &\left\{\mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{j=1}^q
   \left(\left\|\phi'\right\|_\infty
       \left|\mathsf X_{i_j}\left(t\right)-\mathsf X_{i_j}\left(s\right)\right|\right)^{2p_j}
  \right]\right\}^{1/2}
 \left\{\mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{j=1}^q \mathsf I_j\right]\right\}^{1/4}\notag\\
 &\qquad\times
 \left\{\mathbb{E}\left[\left|
  \det\left[\mathfrak F_{\boldsymbol{\zeta},r}
       \left(x_{i_j},\mathsf Z_{i_k}\left(T\right)\right)\right]_{j,k=1}^q
 \right|^4\right]\right\}^{1/4}.
 \label{holder 244}
 \end{align}
 The first factor in \eqref{holder 244} is
 \[
 C_{\mathbf{p}}\left\|\phi'\right\|_\infty^{Q}
 \left|t-s\right|^{Q/2};
 \]

 If \(K\subset[-R,R]\), the Gaussian transition density, uniformly for
 \(0\leq s,t\leq T\), gives
 \[
 \left\{\mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{j=1}^q \mathsf I_j\right]\right\}^{1/4}
 \leq C_{q,T,R}\exp\left\{-c_{T,R}
                  \sum_{j=1}^q x_{i_j}^2\right\}.
 \]
 Expanding the determinant, applying \eqref{eq bound of res}, and then
 integrating the Gaussian variables gives, for every sufficiently small
 \(\eta>0\),
 \[
 \left\{\mathbb{E}\left[\left|
  \det\left[\mathfrak F_{\boldsymbol{\zeta},r}
       \left(x_{i_j},\mathsf Z_{i_k}\left(T\right)\right)\right]_{j,k=1}^q
 \right|^4\right]\right\}^{1/4}
 \leq C_{q,T,\eta}
       \exp\left\{\eta C_{q,T}
                  \sum_{j=1}^q x_{i_j}^2\right\}.
 \]
 Choose \(\eta\) small enough that at least half of the Gaussian decay
 remains.  Summing
 \eqref{holder 244} over distinct roots is finite, uniformly in the
 configuration, by \eqref{uniform gaussian summability}.  Finally sum
 over the finitely many \(q\)'s and compositions of \(Q\).  This proves
 \eqref{even Q moment estimate}.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{remark sum is uniformly bounded}
 The family consisting of all \(\boldsymbol{\xi}^{(N)},\boldsymbol{\xi}\) and all their spatial
 truncations satisfies \eqref{uniform gaussian summability}.  Indeed,
 parameter convergence bounds
 \[
 \sup_N\sum_{\substack{x\in\boldsymbol{\xi}^{(N)}\\\left|x\right|>b}}\frac1{x^2}<\infty,
\]
 and rootwise convergence bounds the number of roots in every compact
 interval.  Since \(\mathrm{e}^{-cx^2}\leq C_c/x^2\) for \(|x|>b\), the assertion
 follows; truncation only decreases the sum.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{condition for complex representation}
 Fix \(r\in\mathbb R\), let
 \(\boldsymbol{\zeta}\in\mathfrak M_b\cap\mathfrak M^0\) be infinite,
 and let \(\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}\) have kernel \(\mathfrak K_{f_r^b(\boldsymbol\zeta)}\).
 Assume the residue bound \eqref{eq bound of res}, with the same
 constants for \(\boldsymbol{\zeta}^{[L]}\).  Then
 \eqref{eq complex representation}, with the sum over all distinct roots
 of \(\boldsymbol{\zeta}\), is valid for every \(Q\in\mathbb N\),
 \(\phi\in\mathcal C_c^1(\mathbb R)\), and \(0\leq s<t\leq T\).
 Moreover the series is absolutely convergent.
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Apply Corollary \ref{complex representation} to
 \(\boldsymbol{\zeta}^{[L]}\).  For a fixed collection of matched roots,
 canonical-product convergence gives
 \[
  f_r^b\left(\boldsymbol\zeta^{\left[L\right]}\setminus\left\{x\right\}\right)
   \longrightarrow f_r^b\left(\boldsymbol\zeta\setminus\left\{x\right\}\right)
  \quad\hbox{in }\boldsymbol{\Upsilon}_b .
 \]
 Proposition \ref{uniform convergence of entire}, evaluated also at the
 nonzero limiting denominator, therefore gives locally uniform convergence
 of every entry of the reduced determinant.  For the majorant, use
 \[
  \left|\phi\left(\mathsf X_i\left(t\right)\right)-\phi\left(\mathsf X_i\left(s\right)\right)\right|^{p}
   \leq \left(2\left\|\phi\right\|_\infty\right)^p
      \mathbf{1}\left\{\mathsf X_i\left(s\right)\in\operatorname{supp}\phi
                    \text{ or }\mathsf X_i\left(t\right)\in\operatorname{supp}\phi\right\}.
 \]
 The indicator and determinant estimates from the proof of Lemma
 \ref{lemma for bound} then give, uniformly in \(L\), the majorant
 \[
       C\exp\left\{-c\sum_jx_{i_j}^2\right\}.
 \]
 The Gaussian summability argument in
 Remark~\ref{remark sum is uniformly bounded} applies to
 $\boldsymbol\zeta$ and its truncations. Thus the majorant is summable
 uniformly in $L$, and the right-hand side converges term by term
 and in absolute value.

 It remains to justify convergence of the unbounded polynomial on the
 left.  Apply Lemma \ref{lemma for bound} with the even exponent
 \(R=2\max\{2,Q\}>Q\).  The resulting uniform higher-moment bound makes
 the \(Q\)-th powers uniformly integrable.
 Theorem \ref{MainTheorem} gives convergence in distribution at the
 positive times, while at time \(0\) the initial configurations converge
 vaguely.  Uniform integrability therefore gives convergence of the
 expectations on the left, proving the stated infinite representation.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- cor-2: body_md -->
\label{cor kol bd phi}
 Under the assumptions of Theorem \ref{theorem path cts}, for every even
 \(Q\geq4\), \(T<\infty\), and
 \(\phi\in\mathcal C_c^1(\mathbb R)\), there is
 \(C_{Q,T,\phi}<\infty\) such that
 \begin{equation}\label{eq B_phi}
 \sup_N\mathbb{E}_{r^{(N)},\boldsymbol{\xi}^{(N)}}\left[
 \left|
  \left\langle\phi,\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}^{(N)}\left(t\right)\right\rangle
  -\left\langle\phi,\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}^{(N)}\left(s\right)\right\rangle
 \right|^Q\right]
 \leq C_{Q,T,\phi}\left|t-s\right|^{Q/2},
 \qquad 0\leq s,t\leq T.
 \end{equation}
 The same estimate holds for all spatial truncations and for the limiting
 configuration.
<!-- end cor-2 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
Proposition \ref{bound of res}, Remark
 \ref{remark sum is uniformly bounded}, Lemma \ref{lemma for bound}, and
 Proposition \ref{condition for complex representation} apply with
 constants uniform in \(N\) and in the truncation level.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
We first construct the asserted continuous versions.  For fixed \(N\),
 the finite systems associated with
 \(\boldsymbol{\xi}^{{(N)},[L]}\) and parameter \(r^{(N)}\) are, by Theorem
 \ref{theorem complex repre}, common-drift transforms of finite Dyson
 Brownian motion and hence have continuous paths.  Proposition
 \ref{bound of res} and Corollary \ref{cor kol bd phi} give estimates
 uniform in \(L\).  Since
 \(f_{r^{(N)}}^b(\boldsymbol{\xi}^{{(N)},[L]})\to
   f_{r^{(N)}}^b(\boldsymbol{\xi}^{(N)})\),
 Theorem \ref{MainTheorem} identifies every positive-time
 finite-dimensional limit with the kernel \(\mathfrak K_{\boldsymbol{\upsilon}^{(N)}}\).
 The same argument applies to \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\).

 We give the tightness argument, including compact containment.  Fix
  \(T<\infty\).  Choose a countable convergence-determining family
  \((\phi_k)_{k\geq1}\subset\mathcal C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)\) for the
  vague topology, put
 \[
  A_k\overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}1+C_{4,T,\phi_k},\qquad
  \psi_k\overset{\mathrm{def}}{=} A_k^{-1/4}\phi_k,
 \]
  and use the resulting compatible vague metric
 \begin{equation*}
  d_T\left(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\nu}\right)
  \overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}\sum_{k=1}^\infty2^{-k}
    \frac{\left|\left\langle\psi_k,\boldsymbol{\mu}
                        -\boldsymbol{\nu}\right\rangle\right|}
         {1+\left|\left\langle\psi_k,\boldsymbol{\mu}
                        -\boldsymbol{\nu}\right\rangle\right|}.
 \end{equation*}
 Jensen's inequality and \eqref{eq B_phi} give
 \begin{equation}\label{Holder}
  \sup_{N,L}
  \mathbb{E}\!\left[
   d_T\left(\boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Xi}}^{{(N)},\left[L\right]}\left(t\right),
